lessons.title: Names remember values
lessons.body: Assignment evaluates the right side, then stores its result under the name on the left. Read = as ‘gets’, not ‘is equal to’.
lessons.code:
coins = 4
print(coins)
lessons.takeaway: The output is 4. Quotes would make coins literal text.

lessons.title: Values have types
lessons.body: Numbers support arithmetic. Quoted text is a string, even when it contains digits. Joining two strings does not add two numbers.
lessons.code:
print(3 + 2)
print("3" + "2")
lessons.takeaway: The outputs are 5 and 32.

lessons.title: Reassign a name
lessons.body: A later assignment replaces the earlier value. Python executes statements from top to bottom.
lessons.code:
coins = 4
coins = coins + 2
print(coins)
lessons.takeaway: The new value is 6; the right side uses the old value.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
gems = 3
gems = gems + 4
print(gems)
questions.feedback: The second assignment reads the old 3, adds 4, and stores 7. Assignment changes the value.

questions.prompt: Now use text instead of coins. What is printed?
questions.code:
label = "2"
label = label + "5"
print(label)
questions.feedback: Both values are strings. + joins their characters to form 25; it does not perform numeric addition.

lessons.title: Copies are not live formulas
lessons.body: Assigning one integer name to another uses the current value. Later reassignment of the source name does not recompute the destination.
lessons.code:
a = 6
b = a
a = 9
print(b)
lessons.takeaway: b remains 6.

lessons.title: Convert deliberately
lessons.body: Convert a numeric string with int before arithmetic. Conversion returns a value; it does not change the original variable unless assigned.
lessons.code:
raw = "8"
amount = int(raw)
print(amount + 1)
lessons.takeaway: raw is still a string; amount is an integer.

lessons.title: Swap without losing a value
lessons.body: A temporary name preserves an old value. Tuple assignment evaluates every right-hand expression before assigning the targets.
lessons.code:
left = 2
right = 9
left, right = right, left
print(left, right)
lessons.takeaway: The outputs are 9 and 2.

questions.prompt: Choose the replacement for ??? that adds one numerically.
questions.code:
raw = "7"
result = ???
print(result)
questions.feedback: Convert raw before adding. Joining first makes 71, while numeric conversion followed by + 1 makes 8.

questions.prompt: A copied value appears in a new situation. What prints?
questions.code:
stock = 12
reserved = stock
stock = 5
print(reserved, stock)
questions.feedback: reserved retains the integer value 12. Reassigning stock does not update reserved.

lessons.title: Evaluate before assigning
lessons.body: All right-hand expressions in a multiple assignment use the old bindings. This matters when one expression refers to a name also being updated.
lessons.code:
a, b = 2, 5
a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)
lessons.takeaway: The result is 5 7, not 5 10.

lessons.title: Aliasing is different from reassignment
lessons.body: Two names can refer to the same mutable list. Mutating the list is visible through both names. Rebinding one name is not a mutation.
lessons.code:
a = [1]
b = a
a.append(2)
a = [9]
print(b)
lessons.takeaway: b sees [1, 2], not [9].

lessons.title: Make an independent outer list
lessons.body: list.copy creates a different outer list. Appending to that copy does not append to the original. Nested elements are still shared by a shallow copy.
lessons.code:
a = [3]
b = a.copy()
b.append(4)
print(a, b)
lessons.takeaway: The lists are [3] and [3, 4].

questions.prompt: What are the final values?
questions.code:
a, b = 3, 7
a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)
questions.feedback: The right side is evaluated with a=3 and b=7 before either target changes.

questions.prompt: Which value survives the rebinding?
questions.code:
pack = [2]
shared = pack
pack.append(5)
pack = [8]
print(shared)
questions.feedback: append mutates the shared list; the later assignment only rebinds pack. shared still refers to [2, 5].

lessons.title: Ask a True or False question
lessons.body: A comparison such as >= produces a boolean. == compares values; = assigns a value.
lessons.code:
keys = 2
print(keys >= 1)
print(keys == 1)
lessons.takeaway: The results are True then False.

lessons.title: Choose one branch
lessons.body: An if/else selects one of two blocks. The colon starts the block; indentation groups its instructions.
lessons.takeaway: Only enter is printed.

lessons.title: Notice the boundary
lessons.body: A strict > excludes equality. >= includes it. Test exactly the threshold before trusting a condition.
lessons.code:
age = 12
print(age > 12)
print(age >= 12)
lessons.takeaway: At the boundary, the two comparisons differ.

questions.prompt: What is printed?
questions.feedback: 4 >= 5 is False, so only the else block runs.

questions.prompt: A gate includes the boundary age. Choose its condition.
questions.code:
age = 10
# Admit every age of 10 or more.
questions.feedback: >= includes 10 and all larger ages. == would incorrectly exclude older explorers.

lessons.title: First matching branch wins
lessons.body: An if/elif/else chain stops at the first true condition. Put more specific thresholds before broader ones.
lessons.takeaway: Only B is printed.

lessons.title: Combine requirements
lessons.body: and requires both tests to be true. or requires at least one. Parentheses make your intended grouping clear.
lessons.code:
has_key = True
has_pass = False
print(has_key and has_pass)
print(has_key or has_pass)
lessons.takeaway: The outputs are False and True.

lessons.title: Separate if statements
lessons.body: Two if statements are checked independently. An elif is only checked when the preceding if was false.
lessons.takeaway: Both messages print.

questions.prompt: Which branch runs?
questions.feedback: The first condition already matches 95. Python skips the elif; reorder the thresholds to award A.

questions.prompt: Choose the test requiring BOTH a key and enough coins.
questions.code:
has_key = True
coins = 2
# Need a key and at least 3 coins.
questions.feedback: and enforces both requirements. or would admit someone satisfying only one.

lessons.title: Short-circuit guards
lessons.body: and stops as soon as its left operand is false. Use that to guard an operation that would otherwise fail.
lessons.code:
divisor = 0
safe = divisor != 0 and 12 / divisor > 2
print(safe)
lessons.takeaway: False is printed without dividing by zero.

lessons.title: Truthiness and returned operands
lessons.body: and and or return operands, not necessarily boolean objects. Empty strings and zero are falsy.
lessons.code:
name = ""
shown = name or "guest"
print(shown)
lessons.takeaway: or returns guest because name is falsy.

lessons.title: Group complex decisions
lessons.body: not binds before and, and binds before or. Parentheses document a requirement and avoid accidental access paths.
lessons.code:
member = False
admin = True
active = False
print((member or admin) and active)
lessons.takeaway: The active requirement applies to both roles.

questions.prompt: Which expression safely checks the quotient?
questions.code:
n = 0
# Do not divide by zero.
questions.feedback: The guard must come first and be False for zero so Python skips the division.

questions.prompt: What value does this store?
questions.code:
nickname = ""
backup = "scout"
name = nickname or backup
print(name)
questions.feedback: or returns the first truthy operand, or the last operand. It returns the string scout here.

lessons.title: Visit a range
lessons.body: range(start, stop) includes start and excludes stop. Think of stop as the first forbidden value.
lessons.code:
for n in range(1, 4):
    print(n)
lessons.takeaway: The outputs are 1, 2, 3 on separate lines.

lessons.title: Repeat a block
lessons.body: Only indented instructions repeat. An instruction after the block runs once after all iterations.
lessons.takeaway: step prints twice; done prints once.

lessons.title: Keep a running total
lessons.body: Initialize before the loop. Each iteration updates the accumulated value.
lessons.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
print(total)
lessons.takeaway: The running totals are 1, 3, and 6.

questions.prompt: What total is printed?
questions.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
print(total)
questions.feedback: range stops before 4, so the sum is 1+2+3=6.

questions.prompt: Choose a range that visits 2, 3, 4, and 5.
questions.code: # The final visited value must be 5.
questions.feedback: Use stop=6 because the stop value is excluded.

lessons.title: Step sizes change visits
lessons.body: range accepts a step. Starting at 1 with a step of 2 visits odd numbers until the excluded stop.
lessons.code: print(list(range(1, 7, 2)))
lessons.takeaway: The values are [1, 3, 5].

lessons.title: A while loop needs progress
lessons.body: A while condition is checked before every iteration. Updating its controlling variable prevents an unintended infinite loop.
lessons.code:
fuel = 3
while fuel > 0:
    fuel -= 1
print(fuel)
lessons.takeaway: The loop stops at 0.

lessons.title: Skip or stop
lessons.body: continue skips the remaining instructions in the current iteration. break exits the loop entirely.
lessons.takeaway: The total is 4 from 0+1+3.

questions.prompt: Where should total = 0 go to accumulate all values?
questions.code:
for n in range(1, 4):
    total = 0
    total += n
print(total)
questions.feedback: Inside the loop it resets on each iteration. Initialize once before the loop to retain earlier additions.

questions.prompt: How many times does this loop execute?
questions.feedback: The body runs with fuel 5, 3, and 1. It then becomes -1 and the next condition is False.

lessons.title: Nested loops multiply work
lessons.body: For each outer value, the inner loop starts again. Count pairs rather than adding the iteration counts.
lessons.takeaway: There are 2×3=6 pairs.

lessons.title: Loop else means no break
lessons.body: A for/else runs its else block only if the loop ends without break, even for an empty iterable.
lessons.takeaway: No break occurs, so the else runs.

lessons.title: Separate filtered accumulation
lessons.body: A filter decides which values contribute; it does not reset the total. Trace both the chosen values and the accumulator.
lessons.takeaway: The contributing a values are 0, 1, 2, 2, giving 5.

questions.prompt: What count is printed?
questions.feedback: Each of the three outer iterations runs the two inner iterations again: 3×2=6.

questions.prompt: What prints for this empty search?
questions.feedback: The iterable is empty, so there is no break. The loop else still executes.

lessons.title: Ordered collections
lessons.body: A list stores an ordered sequence. Indexing starts at zero, so index 1 refers to the second item.
lessons.code:
bag = ["key", "map", "gem"]
print(bag[1])
lessons.takeaway: The output is map.

lessons.title: Length is not the final index
lessons.body: len counts items. A nonempty list's final positive index is len(list)-1.
lessons.code:
bag = ["key", "map"]
print(len(bag))
print(bag[-1])
lessons.takeaway: There are 2 items; the last is map.

lessons.title: Append changes the list
lessons.body: append adds one item at the end of the same list.
lessons.code:
bag = ["key"]
bag.append("gem")
print(bag)
lessons.takeaway: The result is ['key', 'gem'].

questions.prompt: Which item is printed?
questions.code:
bag = ["rope", "key", "map"]
print(bag[1])
questions.feedback: Index 0 is rope and index 1 is key. Python indexes from zero.

questions.prompt: Which expression reads the last item after appending?
questions.code:
bag = ["bread"]
bag.append("water")
questions.feedback: -1 selects the last item. len(bag) is 2, which is beyond the valid positive indices 0 and 1.

lessons.title: Slices exclude the stop
lessons.body: A slice [start:stop] includes start and excludes stop. It returns a new outer list.
lessons.code:
items = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(items[1:3])
lessons.takeaway: The slice is [20, 30].

lessons.title: Methods and return values
lessons.body: append mutates the list and returns None. Do not assign its return value back to the list.
lessons.code:
items = [1]
result = items.append(2)
print(items, result)
lessons.takeaway: items is [1, 2]; result is None.

lessons.title: Transform every item
lessons.body: A comprehension builds a new list from an expression applied to each item. An optional if filters items first.
lessons.code:
values = [1, 2, 3]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in values if n > 1]
print(doubled)
lessons.takeaway: The result is [4, 6].

questions.prompt: Choose a fix that keeps items as a list.
questions.code:
items = [1]
items = items.append(2)
questions.feedback: append mutates items directly and returns None. Remove the assignment to preserve the list binding.

questions.prompt: Which result does this slice produce?
questions.code:
values = [4, 8, 12, 16]
print(values[1:3])
questions.feedback: Indices 1 and 2 are included; the stop index 3 is excluded.

lessons.title: A shallow copy shares inner lists
lessons.body: copy makes a new outer list but keeps references to the same inner objects.
lessons.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)
print(a)
lessons.takeaway: a becomes [[1, 3], [2]] because the inner list is shared.

lessons.title: Avoid mutation while iterating
lessons.body: Removing items shifts later indices. The iterator can skip a value that shifts into an already-visited position.
lessons.code:
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
kept = [n for n in values if n % 2 == 0]
print(kept)
lessons.takeaway: Build a filtered list to avoid skipped items.

lessons.title: Repetition can share references
lessons.body: Repeating a list of mutable objects repeats references, not independent nested copies.
lessons.code:
grid = [[0]] * 2
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)
lessons.takeaway: Both rows show [9]. Use a comprehension for independent rows.

questions.prompt: What is printed?
questions.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(5)
print(a[0])
questions.feedback: The outer copy is independent but the inner list a[0] is shared with b[0].

questions.prompt: Choose two independent rows.
questions.code: # Changing one row should not change the other.
questions.feedback: The comprehension creates a new inner list per iteration; repetition and reusing row share references.

lessons.title: Define, then call
lessons.body: def describes a reusable block. Its body does not run until you call the function.
lessons.takeaway: The call prints hello once.

lessons.title: Parameters receive arguments
lessons.body: A parameter is a local name that receives the supplied argument. Different calls can use different values.
lessons.takeaway: n receives 3 and the result is 6.

lessons.title: Return sends a value back
lessons.body: return provides the call's value. print displays text. A function that finishes without return returns None.
lessons.code:
def add_one(n):
    return n + 1
answer = add_one(4)
print(answer)
lessons.takeaway: The caller receives 5.

questions.prompt: What value is printed?
questions.feedback: The argument 4 becomes n and return sends back 8.

questions.prompt: Choose the body that lets the caller use the result.
questions.feedback: Only return supplies the calculated value to result. Printing or evaluating alone leaves the return value as None.

lessons.title: Local names stay local
lessons.body: Assigning to a parameter rebinds a local name. It does not reassign the caller's integer variable.
lessons.code:
def grow(n):
    n += 2
    return n
size = 3
new_size = grow(size)
print(size, new_size)
lessons.takeaway: The output is 3 5.

lessons.title: Every return path matters
lessons.body: A branch that reaches the end without return produces None. Decide what every possible input should return.
lessons.takeaway: A fallback return covers inputs that miss the if.

lessons.title: Compose results
lessons.body: A function call can be an argument to another call. Evaluate the inner call first.
lessons.takeaway: The inner result is 3 and the final result is 4.

questions.prompt: What is the missing-path result?
questions.feedback: The condition is false and execution reaches the end without return, so the function returns None.

questions.prompt: What remains in the caller?
questions.code:
def bump(n):
    n += 1
    return n
level = 4
next_level = bump(level)
print(level, next_level)
questions.feedback: The parameter n is local. The call returns 5 without rebinding the caller's level.

lessons.title: Defaults are created once
lessons.body: A mutable default is shared across calls. Use None and create a fresh list inside the function when each call should be independent.
lessons.takeaway: The None sentinel avoids a shared default list.

lessons.title: Mutation crosses the boundary
lessons.body: Reassigning a parameter is local. Mutating the object referenced by a parameter can affect the caller.
lessons.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append(7)
bag = [2]
add_item(bag)
print(bag)
lessons.takeaway: The same bag object now contains [2, 7].

lessons.title: Base cases stop recursion
lessons.body: Recursive calls must reach a base case. Each caller resumes with the returned result, so trace calls down and returns up.
lessons.takeaway: The returned sum is 3+2+1+0=6 for nonnegative inputs.

questions.prompt: What prints on the second call?
questions.code:
def collect(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag
collect(1)
print(collect(2))
questions.feedback: The default list was created once and reused. The first call's mutation survives into the second call.

questions.prompt: What does the caller see?
questions.code:
def update(items):
    items.append(3)
    items = [9]
bag = [1]
update(bag)
print(bag)
questions.feedback: append changes the caller's list. The later assignment only rebinds the local parameter.
